You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: NVIDIA FY2027 Q2 Earnings Highlights: Revenue Doubles YoY to $96.2 Billion; Data Center Up 117%; Next-Year Guidance Implies ~70% Growth

TEXT:
Key Takeaways
NVIDIA reported FY2027 Q2 revenue (quarter ended July 26, 2026) of $96.221 billion, up 106% year over year and 18% quarter over quarter. That beat analyst estimates by more than 4% and came in about $5.2 billion above the midpoint of the company’s prior Q2 guidance of $91.0 billion.
Non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $2.22, up 120% YoY and above the $2.09 consensus by nearly 6%.
Data center revenue was $89.0 billion (official figure $89.023 billion), up 117% YoY and accounting for about 92.5% of total revenue.
The company guided FY2027 Q3 revenue to a midpoint of $108.0 billion (±2%), implying nearly 90% YoY growth and the first quarter above $100 billion. Gross margin guidance midpoint, however, stepped down to 74.0%. Guidance “does not assume any data center compute revenue from China.”
On the earnings call, management guided FY2028 revenue growth of about 70%, well above the roughly 45% analyst expectation, and said Amazon AWS will deploy an additional 2 million GPUs in 2027–2028. After hours the stock initially dropped about 4%, then turned higher after the call and was up nearly 5% at one point. Shares had already risen more than 10% in the month leading into the report.
Detailed Breakdown
1. Overall revenue and profit
Revenue: $96.221 billion, +106% YoY, +18% QoQ; highest YoY growth rate since FY2025 Q2.
Prior Q2 revenue guidance midpoint was $91.0 billion; actual result exceeded that by about $5.2 billion.
Non-GAAP net income: $53.954 billion, +118% YoY, +18% QoQ.
Non-GAAP EPS: $2.22 vs. $2.09 expected.
Non-GAAP operating income: $63.956 billion, +124% YoY, above the $61.19 billion analyst estimate; operating margin about 66%.
GAAP net income: $59.688 billion, +126% YoY.
GAAP EPS: $2.46. GAAP exceeded non-GAAP mainly because the quarter included about $7.77 billion of net gains on equity securities (official figure $7.771 billion), which are excluded from non-GAAP profit.
GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75.0%, roughly in line with expectations; up about 2.6 and 2.5 percentage points YoY respectively, and essentially flat QoQ.
Non-GAAP operating expenses: $8.232 billion, below the $8.32 billion estimate.
GAAP operating expenses: $8.408 billion, +55% YoY, +10% QoQ.
Operating cash flow for the quarter: $24.077 billion. Working-capital use rose: accounts receivable increased $22.346 billion, inventory $5.784 billion, and prepaid and other assets $5.497 billion.
About $26 billion was returned to shareholders in the quarter (buybacks and dividends). Next-quarter cash dividend is $0.25 per share; record date September 10, 2026; payment date October 1, 2026.

2. Data center performance
Data center revenue: $89.0 billion (official $89.023 billion), +117% YoY, +18% QoQ, above analyst estimates of roughly $85.8–85.9 billion by nearly 4%.
About 92.5% of total company revenue; the business remains tightly tied to the global AI infrastructure buildout.
Growth was driven mainly by the Blackwell Ultra infrastructure r Blackwell still accounted for the majority of system shipments.
Hyperscale revenue: $48.71 billion, +102% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $43.55 billion estimate.
Compute Networking: $88.3 billion, above the $84.69 billion estimate.
ACIE (AI cloud, industrial and enterprise): $40.31 billion, +138% YoY, +25% QoQ, but below the $41.96 billion market estimate. Official explanation: growth came from AI-native customers, enterprises, sovereign customers, and hyperscalers using AI cloud.
Data center Hopper product shipments to China were less than 1% of data center revenue in the quarter.
CEO Jensen Huang: “AI has reached an inflection point. It is doing useful work. Tokens are becoming productive and profitable. Compute is now revenue.”
A year ago, buildout was driven mainly by one AI lab. Today multiple frontier labs are expanding in parallel, the open-source model ecosystem is thriving, and physical AI is starting to go live.
The Vera Rubin platform has entered full-scale production. Racks are already running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Management expects Rubin to account for about 20% of Q3 data center revenue.
3. Other segments
Edge Computing revenue: $7.2 billion (official $7.198 billion), +27% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $6.61 billion estimate. Covers RTX, Windows on-device AI, robotics, autonomous driving, and is core to the “physical AI” narrative, but remains far smaller than data center.
[...]
Structurally, NVIDIA remains highly dependent on data center in the near term. Edge/graphics is growing but is not yet large enough to change the revenue mix.
[...]
NVIDIA is shifting from selling individual GPUs to system-level delivery of full racks, networking, CPUs, software, and deployment solutions. Rubin is not a single chip; it is an “AI factory” architecture that includes Vera CPU, Rubin GPU, Spectrum-6 networking, BlueField, security, storage, software toolchain, and the DSX platform.
[...]
Responding to “circular financing” questions, Kress said frontier labs such as OpenAI “will become the largest technology companies in history,” face a compute-access bottleneck, and that NVIDIA is providing capital support. “We understand the scale of this support… the capital we put in will generate excellent equity returns.”
[...]
Expanded AWS partnership: on top of the existing plan for about 1 million GPUs, an additional 2 million GPUs will be deployed in 2027–2028 (covering Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra), along with Vera CPUs (some integrated with Rubin, some standalone).
[...]
The stock turned up nearly 5% after the call, driven by the ~70% FY2028 growth guide, the additional 2 million GPUs for AWS, and management’s emphasis that demand is still accelerating and AI has reached a “compute is revenue” inflection.
[...]
